sensitivity_investment_pass_through.note: alpha_inv = Rachel and Smith's 0.2 per point of GDP times the pass-through of the investment fall, per point of income (macro.investment_key): 1 gross (the central), 0.4 net for a growing stock (g / delta), 0 netted against capital consumption; the rest of the refit held; fixed return, the three speeds

units.note: the literature's coefficients are per point of GDP; the model applies them per point of its income, divided once by gdp_over_income (decision 73's units, corrected in Log 54: until then the GDP numbers were applied per point of income unconverted). Not converted: tp_per_debt, debt_threshold, loss_per_debt (illustrative, per point of income since the macro block's first commit, never sourced)

neutral_scale.Rachel and Smith (2015), BoE Staff WP 57: saving elasticity 0.5, investment -0.7 (-0.5 adjusted for the relative price of capital), calibrated: a 1 pp of GDP saving shift ~25 bp, 4 pp ~90 bp; a 4 pp fall in investment ~80 bp; A ~0.20-0.25
neutral_scale.Rachel and Summers (2019), NBER WP 26198: 1 pp lower r widens the saving-investment gap by 2-4 pp of GDP (central 3): A ~0.33 (0.25-0.5)
neutral_scale.Holston, Laubach and Williams (2017), JI: US IS curve a_y 0.942, a_r -0.071: (1 - a_y)/|a_r| 0.82 in output-gap units (multipliers included): an upper bound
neutral_scale.Eggertsson, Mehrotra and Robbins (2019),: a labour-share fall 72.4 -> 66.0% lowers r 0.52 pp (~8 bp per pp: compare alpha_rent); debt +76 pp of GDP raises r 2.11 pp

owners_saving_gap.Onaran and Galanis (2012), ILO, Table 3: C/Y per +1 pp of profit share: US -0.43, euro area -0.44, France -0.31, Germany -0.50
owners_saving_gap.Stockhammer and Wildauer (2016), CJE 40(: +1 pp wage share raises C 0.12 pp of GDP (household debt, property prices held)
owners_saving_gap.Mian, Straub and Sufi (2021), Jackson Ho: saving rates top 10% 25.3%, next 40% 8.2%, bottom 50% 2.6%; the top 10%'s income share +11.8 pp raised saving 2.4 pp of national income: ~0.20 per unit shifted (average group rates)
owners_saving_gap.Mian, Straub and Sufi (2025), NBER WP 26: top 1% saving rate over 40% of disposable income (retained earnings attributed; by wealth group), bottom 50% ~0
owners_saving_gap.Dynan, Skinner and Zeldes (2004), JPE 11: marginal saving between income quintiles 0.03-0.43: cross-section levels on the change in wealth, capital gains included, which they flag as biased up at the top; their time-series estimates (MPS Q5 0.25, change in wealth) put the gap between the top quintile and the bottom three at ~0.16-0.18, which supports the household-only end (0.15-0.20) rather than 0.30
owners_saving_gap.Fagereng, Holm, Moll and Natvik (2019),: net saving rates flat at ~6-8% across wealth (retained earnings in capital gains, outside net saving): the household-only basis gives a smaller gap
owners_saving_gap.Di Maggio, Kermani and Majlesi (2020), J: Swedish MPC out of dividends 0.40-0.60; out of capital gains ~0.03 at the top
owners_saving_gap.basis: the non-wage share includes all owners' income, retained earnings included: the gap on that basis 0.30 (0.15-0.45); household-only 0.15-0.20; all local estimates, applied here to a ~50 pp shift. The horizon as well as the size: the Kaleckian C/Y estimates above (Onaran and Galanis, Hein and Vogel, Onaran and Obst, Stockhammer and Wildauer) are short-run first-difference responses, one on gross profits, whose authors found no long-run level relation; the long-run evidence is mixed — Mian, Straub and Sufi 2021 (~0.20) and Dynan, Skinner and Zeldes's time-series gap (~0.16-0.18) point lower, Mian, Straub and Sufi 2025's top-1% saving rates higher (corrected in Log 54, evidence:A5-A6)

$1 of deficit cuts national saving 50-80 cents (offset 0.2-0.5); a projected primary deficit raises long rates 40-70 bp per pp
deficit_pass_through.R\u00f6hn (2010), OECD ECO WP 762: private saving offsets ~40% of a change in the budget balance on average; changes in current revenues almost fully, changes in current spending one third to one half; the offset is stronger the higher the government's debt
deficit_pass_through.Laubach (2009), JEEA 7(4): ~25 bp per pp of projected deficit / GDP, 3-4 bp per pp of debt, on 5-year-ahead long nominal rates
deficit_pass_through.Rachel and Summers (2019), Table 2: literature averages 38 bp per pp of deficit, 3.5 bp per pp of debt
deficit_pass_through.note: the common scale gives alpha_fiscal = 0.3 x 0.6 = 0.18 pp of r* per pp of GDP of primary deficit, 0.157 per pp of income: it rests on the saving-offset evidence alone (Gale and Orszag, Röhn, de Mello et al.: offsets of a fifth to a half). It lies below every direct long-yield estimate (0.25-0.70 per pp of GDP: Laubach ~25 bp, Rachel and Summers's average 38, Gale and Orszag 40-70), and the sources do not set those aside for carrying term premia and expected inflation: Rachel and Summers apply their 38 bp to R* directly (corrected in Log 54, evidence:A3: the note gave that reason); the direct estimates are decision 74's alternative (0.25-0.5 per pp of GDP). The model's term premium rises with debt above 60% of income on its own (tp_per_debt 0.02: illustrative defaults since the macro block's first commit, 24 Sep 2026, per point of income and never sourced; as the 60%-of-GDP reference the threshold would be ~69% of income, and Laubach's 3-4 bp per pp of debt / GDP is 0.026-0.035 per pp of income, on long nominal yields), which adds to the long-rate response once debt passes it. Röhn's composition and debt-level results pull the other way: this model's deficits are mostly revenue lost as the wage tax's base shrinks (at medium the wage tax's share of revenue falls 0.80 -> 0.11) while debt passes 100% of income, which those results offset more than the average: a pass-through below 0.6 (evidence:A4). The deficits leg is bounded by two strands pulling opposite ways, the yield evidence up and the offset evidence down, and pinned by neither. The deficits branch takes no offset at all (pass-through 1.0: 0.30 per pp of GDP, 0.262 per pp of income): beyond the saving-offset estimates, whose largest pass-through is 0.8 (Gale and Orszag's 80 cents), it stands on the direct yield evidence only

investment_key.Rachel and Smith (2015), BoE Staff WP 57: a 4 pp of GDP fall in investment lowers the neutral rate ~80 bp: 0.2 pp of r* per pp of GDP — their short-termism scenario, an upper bound on what an investment fall alone does; they read gross investment against gross saving
investment_key.Rachel and Summers (2019), NBER WP 26198: the saving-investment gap's scale, 1 pp lower r per 2-4 pp of GDP (A ~0.33)
investment_key.the model's fall: replacement investment / income falls ~13 points by year 15 at the medium and fast speeds (17.8 -> 4.5 and 4.4% of income) and ~7 at the slow (to 10.5%; 8 on the high root), far outside Rachel and Smith's 4 pp: the coefficient is extrapolated (a linear bridge far beyond its evidence)
investment_key.pass_through: how much of the investment fall counts as excess saving: gross 1.0 (Rachel and Smith's reading, the central), net for a growing stock ~0.4 (g / delta of replacement), netted against capital consumption 0 (the model's income is net of replacement investment). The evidence does not pin it: the central is gross and the reverse envelope draws it over 0-1 (macro.INVESTMENT_PASS_THROUGH_RANGE); sensitivity_investment_pass_through runs 1 / 0.4 / 0 on the fixed-return table
investment_key.note: alpha_inv = macro.INVESTMENT_KEY = 0.2 x the pass-through per point of GDP, 0.175 per point of the model's income at the central (gross); before the revision (Log 46) the investment key was the common scale, 0.3, applied per point of income unconverted

fiscal_start.note: the model's deficit is primary and net of property income received (decision 95): interest paid enters debt through r* + pi* - growth, and the model's government has gross debt and no assets, so it receives none; the alternative (start_deficit_alternative) keeps the state's asset income in revenue. In % of income (GDP net of the chain's imported content and of replacement investment); the start is an equilibrium at capacity, so the five-year mean stands in for a structural balance (2022's surplus and 2023-25's slowdown both in it)
